<!-- file: README.md -->

# appdeploy

Deploy web apps to your own servers with `git push`. A small agent on each server builds your
Dockerfile, starts the new version next to the old one, checks it, switches traffic, watches
the real traffic for a few minutes, and **rolls back by itself** if the new version misbehaves.
It keeps going when your laptop disconnects, and picks up where it left off if the agent
itself restarts.

```bash
git remote add prod deploy@my-server:myapp
git push prod main
```

```
remote: ==> validating
remote: ==> building
remote: ==> starting
remote: ==> verifying
remote: myapp-v2-web-1: healthcheck GET /up ok
remote: ==> switching
remote: ==> observing
remote: ==> succeeded: myapp is now serving v2
```

> **Status: early (v0.1).** The core is covered by an end-to-end test suite that runs real
> Docker and Caddy, but appdeploy has not been used in production yet and the install script
> has not been run on a real Linux server. Read [what it does not do](docs/comparison.md#what-appdeploy-does-not-do)
> before you choose it.

## Why appdeploy

- **The server drives the deploy, not your laptop.** Close the lid, lose Wi-Fi, kill `git push`:
  the deploy finishes anyway. If the agent crashes mid-switch, it finishes or reverts on restart.
- **Rollback by real traffic, not just a health check.** After the switch the old version stays
  up while the new one is watched. Too many 5xx, crash loops or failing health checks put
  traffic back on the old version in one proxy switch.
- **No registry, no cross-building.** Images are built on the server (or on a build server)
  and sent between your servers directly.
- **Small groups without Kubernetes.** 1 to about 10 servers: roles placed by labels, canary
  first, a failed rollout is undone, a server that was down catches up by itself.
- **Easy to move in and out.** `appdeploy import kamal` reads a Kamal setup and says what it becomes
  (and what blocks it); `appdeploy export` writes the same setup for Kamal, Docker Compose,
  Kubernetes or Fly. Your app only needs a Dockerfile, environment variables and `GET /up`.
- **Made to be operated by scripts and AI assistants:** `--json` on every command, a local
  `appdeploy check` for the config, and [a guide written for LLMs](docs/llm-guide.md).
- **Batteries for small apps:** Postgres and Redis per app with daily backups, secrets per
  release, webhooks (Slack, Telegram, generic), signed self-update, SSH roles.

How it compares to Kamal, Dokku, Coolify and others: [docs/comparison.md](docs/comparison.md).

## Quick start

On a Debian or Ubuntu server with systemd, as root, with the binary and `install.sh` of one
[release](https://github.com/merkushin/appdeploy/releases) (download steps in
[Getting started](docs/getting-started.md#1-get-the-binary-and-the-install-script)):

```bash
./install.sh --binary ./appdeploy-linux-amd64 --ssh-key-file ./my-key.pub
```

On your computer, with the `appdeploy` binary from the same release:

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server apps create myapp --domain myapp.example.com
git remote add prod deploy@my-server:myapp
git push prod main
```

The full walkthrough, including DNS and what your app must provide, is in
[Getting started](docs/getting-started.md).

## Development

```bash
go test ./...                              # unit tests
go test -tags e2e -timeout 40m ./e2e       # end-to-end: needs Docker; pulls golang:1.27-alpine, caddy:2, postgres and redis
```

The end-to-end tests start their own agent and Caddy, deploy the Go apps in `examples/`, and
remove every container, image, network, volume and directory they create. Set `E2E_KEEP=1`
to keep the temp directory (with `agent.log`) when debugging. The documentation is checked
against the code by `go test ./internal/docs` (commands, configuration keys, agent flags, API
routes, links, examples and the error messages the docs quote); if you change `README.md` or
`docs/`, regenerate `llms-full.txt` with `UPDATE_DOCS=1 go test ./internal/docs`. Releases are described in
[SPEC.md §27](SPEC.md).

<!-- file: docs/llm-guide.md -->

# Guide for AI assistants and agents

For an LLM or an autonomous agent that operates appdeploy on behalf of a person. It is written
to be followed literally. It describes version 0.1.x; if a command here disagrees with
`appdeploy help` on the machine you are on, trust `appdeploy help` and say so.

Files for ingestion: [`llms.txt`](../llms.txt) (an index) and
[`llms-full.txt`](../llms-full.txt) (all the documentation in one file).

## What appdeploy is, in six facts

1. appdeploy deploys **Docker-based web apps** to Linux servers with `git push` or `appdeploy deploy`.
   A deploy is run **by an agent on the server**, not by your terminal.
2. An app is a git repository with a **Dockerfile**. Its settings are an optional `appdeploy.yml`.
3. A deploy builds a **release** (`v1`, `v2`, ...). The old release keeps serving until the new
   one is verified, and for a few minutes after the switch. A failed deploy changes nothing for
   users. The system may **roll back by itself** (`rolled_back`): that is it working, not a bug.
4. **Secrets** are environment variables stored on the server. Releases freeze their secrets.
5. Containers are disposable. Data lives in Postgres/Redis or elsewhere; files that must survive can go in a
   **named volume** (`roles.<name>.volumes: ["data:/data"]`), which is not backed up. Non-secret environment
   goes in `env:` of `appdeploy.yml`, secrets in `secrets set`.
6. The CLI is `appdeploy`. From a workstation: `appdeploy --host deploy@SERVER <command>`. On the
   server itself: `appdeploy <command>` (needs root or the socket group). `--host` may be left out when
   the server comes from `APPDEPLOY_HOST`, `host:` in `appdeploy.yml`, a git remote named `prod` or
   `appdeploy`, or `appdeploy hosts`; the command says on stderr where it took the server from. Do not
   guess a host: when none is known, ask the user.

## Rules

Follow these in order of importance.

1. **Look before you change.** Run `appdeploy --host H status APP` first and say what you saw.
   Never assume an app, a release number or a server exists.
2. **Never judge a deploy by the exit status of `git push`.** It is 0 even when the deploy failed.
   A deploy succeeded only if the output contains `==> succeeded` or `appdeploy deploy` exited 0.
   `deploy failed:` and `rolled back` mean it did not (for `failed`, the old release is still live).
3. **Do not retry blindly.** Read the error line that starts with `deploy failed:` (or `watchdog:`),
   fix the cause, then deploy again. Repeating an unchanged deploy repeats the failure and wastes a
   release number.
4. **Never reveal secrets.** Do not run `secrets export`, and do not run `exec` with commands that print the
   environment (`env`, `printenv`, `cat /proc/*/environ`), unless the person asked for exactly that.
   Use `secrets list` (names only). Never write secret values into files in a repository, logs or
   your answers. Values passed to `secrets set` appear in the shell history: tell the person.
5. **Ask the person first** for anything in the "ask first" rows below. State what will happen, to
   which app and server, and whether it can be undone.
6. **Be patient.** A deploy takes the build time plus a 3-minute watch window by default. Do not
   interrupt it, and do not start a second deploy of the same app to "speed it up": it would only queue behind the
   running one. Use `--detach` and poll `status` every 30 seconds or longer if you must not block.
7. **Do not touch appdeploy's files or containers by hand.** No editing of `/var/lib/appdeploy`, no
   `docker rm` or `docker stop` of containers named `ad-*`, no editing of Caddy's config. Use commands.
8. **Do not invent options.** Only the commands in this documentation exist. If you need something
   that is not here (volumes, buildpacks, an interactive shell), say it is not supported.
9. **Check the docs for what you are not sure about,** and say when you were unsure.

## Command safety

"Role" is the lowest SSH role that may run it (viewer < deployer < admin).

| Command | What it does | Undo | Ask first? | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ping`, `version [--verbose]`, `status`, `apps list`, `releases`, `db list`, `group servers` | read only | n/a | no | viewer |
| `check [FILE]` | validates an `appdeploy.yml` on this machine; no server involved | n/a | no | local |
| `import kamal [FILE]` | reads a Kamal config on this machine and prints a plan; changes nothing | n/a | no (but show the person the blockers) | local |
| `logs APP [--role R] [--tail N]` | prints container logs (may contain personal data) | n/a | no | deployer |
| `secrets list APP` | names of secrets | n/a | no | deployer |
| `export APP --format F` | prints config for another tool (no secret values) | n/a | no | admin |
| `self-update --check` | looks for a newer release | n/a | no | admin |
| `deploy APP`, `deploy APP --ref SHA` | new release of the code; the old one serves until verified | `rollback` | **yes on production** | deployer |
| `deploy APP --image REF` | same, from a prebuilt image | `rollback` | **yes on production** | deployer |
| `redeploy APP` | new release of the same image | `rollback` | yes | deployer |
| `rollback APP [--to N]` | puts an older release back live | `rollback` or `deploy` | **yes** | deployer |
| `secrets set/unset APP ...` | new release with changed environment | `rollback` restores the old values | **yes** | admin |
| `domains set APP ...` | replaces the domain list at once | set it again | **yes** | admin |
| `apps create APP` | registers an app | `apps destroy` | yes | admin |
| `exec APP -- CMD` | runs a command in the live container | depends on CMD | **yes** | admin |
| `db backup APP` | writes a backup file | delete the file | no | admin |
| `db restore APP NAME` | **replaces the database's tables** | only by restoring another backup | **always** | admin |
| `apps destroy APP [--delete-volumes]` | **removes the app, its images, releases and secrets** (the database and the volumes are kept unless `--delete-volumes`) | no | **always** | admin |
| `secrets export APP` | **prints secret values** | n/a | **always, and say where the output goes** | admin |
| `self-update`, `self-update --force` | replaces the binary and restarts the agent | the agent reverts a bad update by itself | **yes** | admin |
| `group set-version V` | every server installs release V, one after another | set another version | **yes** | admin |
| `group invite`, `group remove S` | adds or removes a server | re-invite | **yes** | admin |

Commands that never make sense for you: `agent`, `hook`, `shell`, `recover`; they are run by the
system.

## Recipes

Replace `H` with `deploy@SERVER`, `APP` with the app. After every change, run
`appdeploy --host H status APP` and report the result.

### Deploy a change

1. `git status` and `git log -1`: confirm what will be deployed. Does the repository have a
   `Dockerfile`? Does the app listen on `$PORT` and answer `GET /up`?
2. `git push prod main` (remote `prod` = `deploy@SERVER:APP`). Success is the line `==> succeeded`.
3. If it printed `deploy failed:` the old release is still live: read the message and the log lines
   above it, fix, repeat. If `rolled back`: look at `watchdog:` for the reason.

For scripts, push to a branch that does not deploy and use the exit status:
`git push prod HEAD:refs/heads/ci && appdeploy --host H deploy APP --ref "$(git rev-parse HEAD)"`.

### Roll back

`appdeploy --host H releases APP` (what exists, which is current), then
`appdeploy --host H rollback APP` (previous) or `rollback APP --to N`. Success is
`==> succeeded: APP is now serving vN`. Remember that rolling back also restores that release's secrets.

### Change a secret

`appdeploy --host H secrets set APP NAME=value`. This creates a release without rebuilding. Tell the
person that the value is in the command line. To change several, use `--no-deploy` on all but the
last. Never print the value back.

### Add a domain

`appdeploy --host H domains set APP a.example.com b.example.com`. This **replaces** the list: include
the existing domains (`status APP` shows them). DNS must already point at the server, or HTTPS will
not work.

### Add a worker or a database

Edit `appdeploy.yml`, commit, deploy:

```yaml appdeploy.yml
roles:
  web: {}
  worker:
    cmd: worker          # arguments to the image's ENTRYPOINT
release_command: migrate
services:
  postgres: true         # provides DATABASE_URL
```

Run `appdeploy check appdeploy.yml` before you commit: it uses the parser of the deploy and reports
every mistake at once (it does not know the server's free memory or disk). An invalid file also
fails in the `validating` step of a deploy, before anything is built or changed, so a mistake is
cheap. Unknown keys are errors: use only the keys in [Configuration](configuration.md).

### Back up and restore a database

`db backup APP` then `db list APP`. To restore, first **ask**, then take a fresh backup, then
`db restore APP NAME`. Backups are on the server's disk only.

### Run a one-off command

`appdeploy --host H exec APP -- COMMAND ARGS`. There is no terminal: nothing interactive. The
command has to exist in the image. Do not use it to read secrets.

### Look at a problem

1. `status APP`: is the container `running`? what did the last deploys end with?
2. `logs APP --tail 100`.
3. On the server: `systemctl status appdeployd appdeploy-caddy`, `journalctl -u appdeployd -n 100`.
4. Match the message in [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

### Update appdeploy

`self-update --check`, tell the person, then `self-update`. For several servers: on the founder,
`group set-version vX.Y.Z`, then watch `group servers`. A version that fails to start reverts itself.

## Reading the output

- A deploy prints `queued`, then lines starting with `==> ` that name the state (`validating`,
  `building`, `migrating`, `starting`, `verifying`, `switching`, `observing`, `succeeded`). Failures print `deploy failed: REASON`. Under `git push` each line is prefixed `remote:`.
- Exit status of `appdeploy`: 0 success; 1 failure (including a deploy that did not succeed); 2 wrong
  usage. The exit status of `git push` is **not** a signal.
- Terminal states of a deploy: `succeeded`, `failed` (old release still live), `rolled_back` (old
  release live again), `superseded` (a newer deploy replaced a waiting one).
- **Ask for JSON.** Add `--json` to any command (`appdeploy --host H status APP --json`): lists and
  objects come as one JSON line, a deploy as one JSON line per journal entry whose last line is
  `{"done":true,"state":"succeeded"|"failed"|"rolled_back"|"superseded","error":"..."}`, and errors as
  `{"error":"..."}`. Parse that, not the text tables, which may change. It works over `--host` for every role.
- On the server you can also use the JSON API directly:

```bash
curl -s --unix-socket /run/appdeploy/agent.sock http://agent/v1/apps/APP | jq '.app.current_release, .containers, .deploys[0]'
curl -s --unix-socket /run/appdeploy/agent.sock http://agent/v1/deploys/DEPLOY_ID
```

  Fields and endpoints: [HTTP API](api.md). Wait for a deploy by reading
  `GET /v1/deploys/ID/events` until a line with `"done":true`.

## Things that look wrong but are normal

- The first deploy of an app is quick and has no `observing`: there is no old release to compare.
- Release numbers skip: a failed deploy uses its number (`v1`, then `v3`).
- A deploy "hangs" for three minutes at `observing`: that is the watch window; traffic has already moved.
- `git push` prints `remote: appdeploy: deploy failed: ...` and still exits 0.
- After a successful deploy the previous container disappears; the release is kept for rollback.
- `status` shows a container of two releases for a few minutes during `observing`.
- Pushing a branch that is not the deploy branch prints `not deploying` and does nothing.

## Not supported: say so, do not improvise

Host directory mounts, volume drivers and backups of volumes; buildpacks (a Dockerfile is required); interactive shells or consoles;
Windows servers; more than about ten servers; a web UI; off-site backups; automatic import from
tools other than Kamal (`appdeploy import kamal` exists; for others see [Migration](migration.md) for the
manual steps, and `appdeploy export` for leaving).

## Defaults worth knowing

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| Deploy branch | `main` |
| Web port | `EXPOSE` of the image, else `8080` (also passed as `$PORT`) |
| Health check | `GET /up`, 2xx or 3xx, up to 60 s to start |
| Memory / CPU per container | 512M / 1 |
| Watch window after the switch | 3 minutes (roll back above 2% 5xx with at least 20 requests, after 2 restarts, or 3 failed health checks) |
| Releases kept | 5 |
| Stop timeout | 30 s |
| Backups | daily, newest of 7 days and 4 weeks, on the server |
| Docker image of release N | `ad/APP:vN` |
| Agent socket | `/run/appdeploy/agent.sock` |

<!-- file: docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

This takes you from an empty server to a deployed app with HTTPS. Plan 15 minutes.

## What you need

- A **server**: Debian or Ubuntu with systemd, root access over SSH, and ports 22, 80 and 443
  reachable. About 1 GB of RAM is enough for a small app; builds need more (a Go or Rails
  build can use 2 GB). appdeploy installs Docker and Caddy for you.
- A **domain name** whose DNS `A` record points at the server. Let's Encrypt needs ports 80
  and 443 to issue the certificate.
- An **app** in a git repository with a `Dockerfile` at the root. See
  [what your app must provide](#3-what-your-app-must-provide).
- On your computer: `git`, `ssh` and the `appdeploy` binary (below).

> The install script has not yet been run on a real server by its authors. It is short and
> plain shell: read it first (`scripts/install.sh`), and expect to report problems.

## 1. Get the binary and the install script

Pick a release (here `v0.1.1`; see the [releases page](https://github.com/merkushin/appdeploy/releases))
and download the binary for the server, its checksums, and the install script **of the same
version**:

```bash
VERSION=v0.1.1
BASE=https://github.com/merkushin/appdeploy/releases/download/$VERSION
curl -fsSLO $BASE/appdeploy-linux-amd64
curl -fsSLO $BASE/SHA256SUMS
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/merkushin/appdeploy/$VERSION/scripts/install.sh
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS      # on macOS: shasum -a 256 -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
chmod +x appdeploy-linux-amd64 install.sh
```

Read `install.sh` before you run it; it runs as root. For your **own computer** download the
matching binary (`appdeploy-darwin-arm64`, `appdeploy-darwin-amd64` or `appdeploy-linux-arm64`),
rename it to `appdeploy` and put it on your `PATH`.

**Check where it came from.** The checksum only proves the download is intact. Each release binary
also carries a build attestation: proof that it was built by this repository's release workflow
and not uploaded from somewhere else. Verify it with the GitHub CLI:

```bash
gh attestation verify appdeploy-linux-amd64 --repo merkushin/appdeploy
```

(Releases made before attestations were added, up to v0.1.1, do not have one.) The release notes
also print the fingerprint of the key the binary will trust for updates. After installing, compare:

```bash
appdeploy version --verbose      # shows the release key and its fingerprint
```

From then on, `appdeploy self-update` accepts only releases signed with that key, so the first
download is the one you verify by hand.

## 2. Install on the server

Copy the files and your **public** SSH key to the server and run the script as root:

```bash
scp appdeploy-linux-amd64 install.sh ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub root@my-server:
ssh root@my-server ./install.sh --binary ./appdeploy-linux-amd64 --ssh-key-file ./id_ed25519.pub
```

The script installs git, Docker and Caddy, puts the binary in `/usr/local/bin/appdeploy`,
creates a user `deploy` whose only SSH ability is to run appdeploy, and starts two services:
`appdeployd` (the agent) and `appdeploy-caddy`. It is safe to run again. Keys you pass with
`--ssh-key` or `--ssh-key-file` are **admins**; add teammates with fewer rights using
`--deployer-key` (can push, deploy, roll back, read logs) or `--viewer-key` (can only look).
See [Operations: security](operations.md#security).

It does not change your firewall or `sshd_config`. Allow 22, 80 and 443 and nothing else.

Check that it works from your computer:

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server ping
```

No output and exit status 0 means the agent answered.

Typing `--host` every time is optional. Say where your server is once, in one of these places
(details in [Commands](commands.md#choosing-the-server)):

```bash
appdeploy hosts add my-server deploy@my-server    # saved on this computer; the first one is the default
# or: host: deploy@my-server        in appdeploy.yml of the project
# or: git remote add prod deploy@my-server:myapp   (the remote named prod or appdeploy)
appdeploy ping                                      # now without --host
```

The rest of this guide keeps `--host` in the examples so that each command stands alone.

## 3. What your app must provide

appdeploy runs your app as a container built from your Dockerfile, and needs three things:

1. **A `Dockerfile` at the repository root** (or set `build.dockerfile` / `build.context` in
   [`appdeploy.yml`](configuration.md)). There are no buildpacks.
2. **Listen on `$PORT`** (default 8080; or `EXPOSE` a port in the Dockerfile, or set
   `roles.web.port`). Listen on all interfaces, not just `localhost`.
3. **Answer `GET /up` with a 2xx or 3xx status** once the app is ready. The new version only
   gets traffic after this passes twice in a row. Use another path with
   `roles.web.healthcheck.path`.

Also good to know: stop cleanly on `SIGTERM` (you get 30 seconds, `roles.web.stop_timeout`),
keep state in a database or in a named volume (`roles.<name>.volumes`), not in the container's
own file system, and read configuration from environment variables (`env:` in `appdeploy.yml`
for the ones that are not secret). A minimal example is in
[`examples/hello`](../examples/hello).

## 4. Create the app and deploy

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server apps create myapp --domain myapp.example.com
```
```
created app myapp (deploy branch main)
  git remote add prod <user>@<server>:myapp
  git push prod main
```

In your project:

```bash
git remote add prod deploy@my-server:myapp
git push prod main
```

You see the deploy as it happens, prefixed with `remote:`. The first deploy builds the image
and takes a while:

```
remote: queued (push)
remote: ==> validating
remote: commit 7e27d62d (no appdeploy.yml: using defaults)
remote: memory: 0B reserved + 512.0MiB for this release of 13.3GiB available
remote: ==> building
remote: ==> starting
remote: started ad-myapp-v1-web-1 (role web)
remote: ==> verifying
remote: ad-myapp-v1-web-1: healthcheck GET /up ok
remote: ==> switching
remote: ==> succeeded: myapp is now serving v1
```

Visit `https://myapp.example.com`. The certificate is requested on the first request and can
take a few seconds.

**Important:** `git push` exits with status 0 even when the deploy fails, because git ignores
what the server's hook reports after accepting your push. Read the `remote:` lines, or in
scripts and CI use `appdeploy deploy` (below), which exits non-zero on failure.

Watch the state at any time:

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server status myapp
```
```
myapp  release v1  domains: myapp.example.com

CONTAINER          ROLE  RELEASE  STATE
ad-myapp-v1-web-1  web   v1       running

Recent deploys:
2026-11-14 03:09:06  v1  push  succeeded
```

## 5. Configure it

Put a file `appdeploy.yml` in the repository root only when the defaults do not fit. Every
setting is optional ([full reference](configuration.md)):

```yaml appdeploy.yml
roles:
  web:
    memory: 256M
    healthcheck:
      path: /healthz
  worker:
    cmd: worker            # the image's ENTRYPOINT gets this as arguments
    memory: 128M
release_command: migrate   # runs once, before traffic moves
services:
  postgres: true           # gives the app DATABASE_URL and daily backups
```

Secrets and environment variables are set from the command line and stored on the server:

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server secrets set myapp SESSION_SECRET=... STRIPE_KEY=...
```

This makes a new release (without rebuilding) so the running app picks them up; add
`--no-deploy` to store them for the next release instead.

## 6. Day to day

```bash
git push prod main                                   # deploy
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server logs myapp -f      # follow logs
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server releases myapp     # list releases
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server rollback myapp     # back to the previous release
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server exec myapp -- <command>   # run a command in the running container (no terminal)
```

For deploying from CI, see [Operations: deploying from CI](operations.md#deploying-from-ci).

## Next

- How it works, and why a deploy takes about three minutes: [Concepts](concepts.md)
- All commands: [Commands](commands.md)
- More than one server: [Server groups](groups.md)
- Something went wrong: [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)
- Coming from another tool: [Migration](migration.md)
