<!-- file: docs/concepts.md -->

# Concepts

## The pieces

- **The agent** (`appdeploy agent`, service `appdeployd`) runs on every server as root. It owns
  the state, runs deploys, talks to Docker and Caddy, and answers the CLI over a unix socket.
- **Caddy** (service `appdeploy-caddy`) is the reverse proxy and gets the TLS certificates. The
  agent reconfigures it through its admin API. It is a separate process, so restarting the agent
  never interrupts traffic.
- **Docker** runs your containers. appdeploy uses the `docker` command line.
- **The CLI** is the same binary. `appdeploy --host deploy@server <command>` runs the command
  on the server over SSH; the server side of that is a *forced command*, so the SSH user can do
  nothing but run appdeploy (see [Operations: security](operations.md#security)).
- **git**: each app has a bare repository on the server. Pushing to its deploy branch starts a
  deploy through a `post-receive` hook.

## Apps, roles, releases

An **app** is something you deploy: a name, domains, a git repository, secrets and a config.

A **role** is one kind of process of the app. `web` is special: it gets HTTP traffic, a health
check and the domains. Any other role (`worker`, `jobs`, ...) is just a command that must keep
running. Roles can be placed on different servers with [labels](groups.md).

A **release** is one deployable version: an image, the configuration it was deployed with and a
frozen copy of the app's secrets. Releases are numbered `v1`, `v2`, ... and the numbers never
repeat (a failed deploy uses up its number, so you can see `v1`, `v3`). The last five releases
(`keep_releases`) are kept so you can roll back to them.

Because a release freezes its secrets, **rolling back also restores the old secrets**.

## What happens in a deploy

A deploy is a state machine run by the agent. Every step is written to the agent's journal
*before* it runs, which is how it survives crashes. Your terminal only watches.

| State | What happens |
|---|---|
| `queued` | Waiting. Deploys of one app run one at a time; if several wait, only the newest runs and the others become `superseded`. |
| `validating` | Reads the commit and its `appdeploy.yml`, checks memory (the sum of container limits must fit in RAM minus a reserve) and disk. |
| `building` | `docker build` from your Dockerfile. Builds run one at a time per server. |
| `migrating` | Only if `release_command` is set: runs it once in a throwaway container of the new image, **before** any traffic moves. |
| `starting` | Starts the new containers next to the old ones. |
| `verifying` | Probes `GET /up` of each new web container until it answers 2xx/3xx twice in a row (up to `healthcheck.start_period`), then any `smoke` paths. Worker roles must stay up a few seconds. |
| `switching` | One proxy change moves the domains to the new containers. The old ones keep running. |
| `observing` | The **watchdog** (below) watches the new release for `watch.window`. |
| `succeeded` | The old release is stopped and removed; old images beyond `keep_releases` are pruned. |
| `failed` | Something went wrong **before** traffic moved: the new containers, image and release are removed; the old release never stopped serving. |
| `rolled_back` | The watchdog moved traffic back to the old release and removed the new one. |

So a deploy normally takes the build time plus the observation window, **3 minutes by
default**. Lower it with `watch.window` if that is too long for you; the deploy has already
switched traffic by then, so the wait is only for the safety net.

## The watchdog

After the switch the previous release stays running. For `watch.window` the agent counts
responses of the new release from Caddy's access log and watches its containers. It rolls back
(by switching the proxy, so it is immediate) if:

- more than `max(watch.error_rate, 2 x the previous release's error rate)` of the requests got
  a 5xx answer, with at least `watch.min_requests` requests (needs the access log, which the
  install script configures);
- a container restarted `watch.max_restarts` times or exited;
- the health check fails three times in a row.

The first deploy of an app has nothing to go back to, so it completes at once. Latency is not
watched.

## Migrations and the old version

`release_command` (for example `bin/rails db:migrate`) runs before the switch. While it and
the new containers start, **the old release is still serving**, and after a rollback it serves
again. So migrations must work with the old code too: add a column first, remove the old one in
a later release. appdeploy does not run down-migrations.

If the old release starts failing right after the migration (more 5xx than before), the deploy
does not stop, because the migration is already applied and the new code is the fastest fix. It
logs `WARNING migration.suspect` and sends a webhook so a human knows why.

## Crash safety

- Killing `git push` does not stop the deploy; the agent runs it.
- If the agent dies or restarts mid-deploy, it resumes the deploy from the journal (a build
  starts again, mostly from cache; a switch is completed or reverted).
- The agent is not in the traffic path, so restarting or updating it does not affect running
  apps.

## State

Everything the agent knows is under `/var/lib/appdeploy` (see
[Configuration: files on disk](configuration.md#files-on-disk)): a SQLite database with apps,
releases and the deploy journal, the git repositories, secrets (mode 0600) and backups.

## Where appdeploy has opinions

- Containers are disposable. Persistent data belongs in Postgres, Redis (appdeploy can run both
  for you, with backups) or an external service; files that must survive can go in a **named
  volume** (`roles.<name>.volumes`), which is not backed up and is shared by the old and the new
  release until the watch window ends.
- You provide a Dockerfile. appdeploy never guesses a build.
- One web port per app, one proxy per server. Spreading traffic across several servers is up to
  a load balancer in front; each server answers `GET /health/<app>` for it.

---

<!-- file: docs/commands.md -->

# Commands

```
appdeploy [--host user@host|name] [--socket path] <command> [arguments]
```

- **`--host user@host`** runs the command on that server over SSH. Without any server (see
  [Choosing the server](#choosing-the-server)) the command talks to the agent on this machine.
- **`--socket path`** (or `APPDEPLOY_SOCKET`) is the agent's socket, default
  `/run/appdeploy/agent.sock`. You need it only when running on the server yourself.
- **Exit status:** `0` success, `1` the command failed (an error is printed to stderr, a deploy
  that did not succeed counts as a failure), `2` wrong usage.
- **Roles.** Over SSH, what you may run depends on your key's role: a *viewer* can run the
  read-only commands, a *deployer* adds deploy, rollback and logs, an *admin* can run everything.
  The tables below say which. See [Operations: security](operations.md#security).

- **`--json`** (anywhere before a `--`) prints JSON instead of text, for scripts and AI assistants:
  one line per object or list; for a deploy one JSON line per journal entry, the last being
  `{"done":true,"state":"succeeded","error":""}`; errors as `{"error":"message"}` on stdout. It works
  over `--host` and for every role. Fields are those of the [HTTP API](api.md). Commands that print
  free text (`logs`, `exec`) ignore it.

Most commands that change something stream the agent's journal until the deploy ends, so you
see what a `git push` shows. Press Ctrl-C to stop watching; **the deploy continues on the server**
(its id is printed so you can look it up).

## Choosing the server

A command runs on the first server found in this list:

1. `--host user@host`, or `--host NAME` for a name defined in `hosts:` of `appdeploy.yml` or saved
   with `appdeploy hosts add`;
2. the environment variable `APPDEPLOY_HOST` (an address or a name);
3. `host: user@host` in the `appdeploy.yml` of the current directory; or its `hosts:` map when it
   has exactly one entry (with several, you must choose one with `--host NAME`);
4. the URL of the git remote named `appdeploy`, then `prod`, in the current directory
   (`deploy@host:app` or `ssh://deploy@host/app`; a URL with a port is not used);
5. the default of `appdeploy hosts`;
6. otherwise the agent on this machine.

When the server comes from 3, 4 or 5, the command prints `appdeploy: using the server ... (from
...)` on stderr, so a repository you cloned cannot send you somewhere unnoticed. An address is
checked: it may not start with `-` or contain spaces.

## appdeploy hosts

```
appdeploy hosts [list]
appdeploy hosts add <name> <user@host> [--default]
appdeploy hosts remove <name>
```

Servers saved on this computer in `~/.config/appdeploy/hosts.yml` (the user configuration
directory of your system; `APPDEPLOY_HOSTS_FILE` overrides the path). The first server added is
the default. Works without a server. Local.

## Reading

| Command | Role | |
|---|---|---|
| [`appdeploy ping`](#appdeploy-ping) | viewer | is the agent up |
| [`appdeploy hosts`](#appdeploy-hosts) | local | servers saved on this computer |
| [`appdeploy check`](#appdeploy-check) | local | validate an `appdeploy.yml` |
| [`appdeploy import kamal`](#appdeploy-import-kamal) | local | turn a Kamal setup into appdeploy's |
| [`appdeploy status`](#appdeploy-status) | viewer | what runs |
| [`appdeploy apps list`](#appdeploy-apps-list) | viewer | all apps |
| [`appdeploy releases`](#appdeploy-releases) | viewer | releases of an app |
| [`appdeploy logs`](#appdeploy-logs) | deployer | container logs |
| [`appdeploy secrets list`](#appdeploy-secrets) | deployer | names of secrets |
| [`appdeploy db list`](#appdeploy-db-backup-list-restore) | viewer | backups of an app |
| [`appdeploy group servers`](#appdeploy-group) | viewer | servers of a group |
| [`appdeploy version`](#appdeploy-version) | any | version of this binary |

## appdeploy ping

Exits 0 and prints nothing if the agent answers.

## appdeploy status

```
appdeploy status [<app>]
```

Without an app: the list of apps (same as `apps list`). With an app: its live release,
domains, containers with their state (and restart counts) and the last five deploys.

```
shop  release v2  domains: shop.example.com

CONTAINER               ROLE  RELEASE  STATE
adocs498-shop-v2-web-1  web   v2       running

Recent deploys:
2026-11-14 03:09:21  v2  rollback  succeeded
2026-11-14 03:09:16  v3  push      succeeded
2026-11-14 03:09:14  v1  rollback  succeeded
```

A deploy's *source* is `push`, `cli` (`appdeploy deploy`), `redeploy`, `rollback`, `image`
(`deploy --image`); in a group also `peer`, `build` and `undo` (work a coordinator asked this
server to do). Deploy states are in [Concepts](concepts.md#what-happens-in-a-deploy).

## appdeploy apps create

```
appdeploy apps create <app> [--domain <domain>]... [--branch main]
```

Registers an app and creates its git repository. The name is lowercase letters, digits and
dashes, starting with a letter, at most 32 characters. Repeat `--domain` for several domains.
`--branch` is the branch that deploys when pushed (default `main`; an `appdeploy.yml` `branch:`
overrides it). Fails if the app exists. **Admin.**

```
created app shop (deploy branch main)
  git remote add prod <user>@<server>:shop
  git push prod main
```

## appdeploy apps list

```
APP   RELEASE  DOMAINS
shop  v1       shop.example.com
```

## appdeploy apps destroy

```
appdeploy apps destroy <app> [--delete-volumes]
```

**Destructive.** Stops and removes the app's containers, removes its images, network, git
repository, releases, secrets and routes. It **keeps** the app's Postgres database and role and
its backups (delete them by hand if you want them gone), and its **volumes**, unless you pass
`--delete-volumes`; the message lists the volumes that stay. Refuses while a deploy is running.
**Admin.**

## appdeploy deploy

```
appdeploy deploy <app> [--ref <sha-or-ref>] [--detach]
appdeploy deploy <app> --image <image> [--config appdeploy.yml] [--detach]
```

Deploys without a push. Without `--ref` it deploys the head of the app's deploy branch in the
server's repository. `--ref` takes a commit that is already in the server's repository (push it
to another branch first). The command waits and **exits non-zero if the deploy did not
succeed**, which makes it the right tool for scripts and CI. `--detach` prints the deploy id and
returns.

`--image` deploys a finished image instead of building one: the server uses it if Docker has it,
otherwise pulls it (a private registry needs `docker login` on the server). `--config` sends an
`appdeploy.yml` to use (`--config -` reads it from standard input; a file name is read on the
machine where the command runs, which with `--host` is the server); without it the config of the live release is reused, or the defaults on a
first deploy. **Deployer.**

## appdeploy redeploy

```
appdeploy redeploy <app> [--detach]
```

New release from the **current image** with the **current secrets**: no build. Use it to pick up
changes made with `secrets set --no-deploy`. **Deployer.**

## appdeploy rollback

```
appdeploy rollback <app> [--to <N>] [--detach]
```

Re-activates an older release: by default the newest one older than the current. It starts the
old image again (with the secrets and config that release had), verifies it, switches traffic
and stops the newer release. It does not create a new release number and is not watched by the
watchdog. If the image of that release was pruned, it fails. In a group it goes back on every
server. **Deployer.**

## appdeploy releases

```
RELEASE  COMMIT    CREATED              
v3       75965914  2026-11-14 03:09:17  <- current
v2       7e27d62d  2026-11-14 03:09:10  
v1       7e27d62d  2026-11-14 03:09:08  
```

## appdeploy logs

```
appdeploy logs <app> [--role <role>] [-f] [--tail <N>]
```

Logs of the containers of the live release, every line prefixed with the container's name.
`--tail` lines per container (default 100), `-f` to follow, `--role` to pick one role.
Containers keep at most three 20 MB log files. **Deployer.**

## appdeploy exec

```
appdeploy exec <app> [--role <role>] -- <command> [arguments...]
```

Runs a command inside a running container of the live release (the first one of the role,
default `web`). Output is streamed; the exit status is the command's. There is **no terminal**:
no interactive shells or consoles. The command must exist in your image. **Admin.**

## appdeploy secrets

```
appdeploy secrets set <app> KEY=value... [--no-deploy]
appdeploy secrets unset <app> KEY... [--no-deploy]
appdeploy secrets list <app>
appdeploy secrets export <app>
```

Secrets are environment variables stored on the server (file mode 0600). `KEY` is letters,
digits and underscores, not starting with a digit; values must be one line.

- `set` and `unset` create a **new release without rebuilding** so running containers get the
  change, and stream it like a deploy. With `--no-deploy` they only store the change for the
  next release (use `redeploy` to apply it).
- `list` prints names only. **Deployer.**
- `export` prints `KEY=value` lines **with values**. It exists to take your secrets with you
  when migrating. **Admin.**
- `set` and `unset` are **admin**.

A secret with the same name as a generated variable (`DATABASE_URL`, `REDIS_URL`) wins, which is
how an app is pointed at an external database. Values given on the command line are visible in
your shell history and the process list while the command runs.

## appdeploy domains set

```
appdeploy domains set <app> <domain>...
```

Replaces the app's domains and reconfigures the proxy at once; no deploy. Domains from
`appdeploy.yml` (`domains:`) are added to these. **Admin.**

## appdeploy export

```
appdeploy export <app> --format kamal|compose|k8s|fly [--out <dir>]
```

Writes the live release's setup in the format of another tool: roles, ports, limits, health
path, domains, the names of secrets (never values) and servers by label. Without `--out` the files
are printed with `==> path <==` headers. See [Migration](migration.md#leaving-appdeploy).
**Admin.**

## appdeploy db backup, list, restore

```
appdeploy db backup <app>
appdeploy db list <app>
appdeploy db restore <app> <backup-name>
```

For apps with `services: {postgres: true}`. `backup` runs `pg_dump` now into
`/var/lib/appdeploy/backups/<app>/<UTC time>.sql.gz` and applies the retention (the newest of each
of the last 7 days and of the last 4 weeks). The agent also backs up every app daily. `list`
prints names, newest first. **`restore` replaces the tables of the app's database with the
backup's.** `list` is viewer; `backup` and `restore` are **admin**. Backups stay on the server's
disk: copy them elsewhere.

## appdeploy group

See [Server groups](groups.md) for the concepts.

```
appdeploy group init --server <name> --advertise <host:port> [--labels web,db] [--group <name>] [--data-dir <dir>]
appdeploy group join --token <token> --server <name> --advertise <host:port> [--labels web] [--data-dir <dir>]
appdeploy group invite
appdeploy group servers
appdeploy group set-version <vX.Y.Z | none>
appdeploy group remove <name>
```

- `init` and `join` run **locally, before the agent starts** (they prepare the server's
  identity under the data directory); the others talk to the agent.
- `invite` (founder only) prints a command to run on the new server; the token works once, for
  one hour.
- `servers` lists members with their labels, agent version and state.
- `set-version` (founder only) makes every server install that release, one at a time, in name
  order. `none` clears it.
- `remove` (founder only) drops a server from the group.

Everything except `servers` is **admin**; `servers` is viewer.

## appdeploy self-update

```
appdeploy self-update [--check] [--force] [--repo owner/name]
```

Asks the agent to install the latest GitHub release if it is newer and correctly signed, then
restart. `--check` only reports. `--force` allows the same or an older version and installing
while deploys are running. See [Operations: updating](operations.md#updating-appdeploy).
**Admin.**

## appdeploy check

```
appdeploy check [<file>] [--json]
```

Validates an `appdeploy.yml` **on your machine, without a server**, with the same parser a deploy
uses, and prints every mistake at once (unknown keys, bad sizes and durations). Without a file it
checks `appdeploy.yml` in the current directory; if there is none, the defaults apply and it says
so. It cannot know the server's limits (free memory, disk): those are checked when you deploy.
Exit status 0 if valid, 1 if not, 2 for a wrong option. With `--json`:
`{"valid":true,"file":"appdeploy.yml","config":{...}}` where `config` is the file with every default
filled in, or `{"valid":false,"file":...,"error":"..."}`.

## appdeploy import kamal

```
appdeploy import kamal [<config/deploy.yml>] [--secrets <file>] [--out <appdeploy.yml>] [--force] [--json]
```

Reads a Kamal setup **on your machine** and prints what it becomes on appdeploy; it changes nothing
on any server and never reads secret values (`.kamal/secrets` is read only for the names). The
report has the generated `appdeploy.yml` (checked by the same parser as `check`), then:

- **BLOCKERS**: things that stop the app from running on appdeploy as it is, such as Kamal `volumes`
  (directories of the host; named volumes are converted) or accessories other than Postgres and Redis;
- **NOT CARRIED OVER**: settings with no equivalent (per-role environment, `env.tags`, proxy
  tuning, builder secrets, ...);
- **TO DECIDE OR CHECK**: things that differ (the app name, the registry, non-secret environment
  that becomes the `env:` section, the volumes to copy data into, secrets named in `.kamal/secrets` but not used);
- **COMMANDS**: `apps create`, `secrets set` (names, with your environment's values), and the git
  remote, in order.

Exit status is 1 when there are blockers, so a script can stop. `--out` writes the
`appdeploy.yml` (it refuses to overwrite without `--force`). With `--json` the whole report is one
object: `verdict` (`ready`, `ready-with-notes`, `blocked`), `appdeploy_yml`, `commands`, `blockers`,
`unsupported`, `notes`. Read [Migration](migration.md#from-kamal) next.

## appdeploy version

```
appdeploy version [--verbose]
```

Prints `appdeploy <version>` (`dev` for a build that did not come from a release). `--verbose` also
prints the repository updates come from and the **release key** this binary trusts, with its SHA-256
fingerprint, to compare with the one in the release notes (see
[Getting started](getting-started.md#1-get-the-binary-and-the-install-script)). With `--json`:
`{"version","update_repository","release_key","release_key_fingerprint"}`.

## appdeploy agent, hook, shell, recover

Used by the system, not by you:

- `appdeploy agent [flags]` runs the agent ([flags](configuration.md#agent-flags)).
- `appdeploy hook post-receive` is called by git after a push.
- `appdeploy shell` is the SSH forced command.
- `appdeploy recover` runs before each start of the service and puts the old binary back after
  a failed update.

---

<!-- file: docs/configuration.md -->

# Configuration

There are three places to configure things:

1. [`appdeploy.yml`](#appdeployyml) in your repository: how an app is built and run.
2. Commands: secrets, domains, apps ([Commands](commands.md)).
3. [Agent flags](#agent-flags): how a server's agent behaves; set once when installing.

## appdeploy.yml

An optional file at the root of your repository. It is read **from the commit being deployed**,
so a config change is an ordinary commit. Unknown keys are an error (a typo cannot be silently
ignored). With no file, all defaults apply: one `web` role.

```yaml appdeploy.yml
app: shop                    # informational; a warning if it differs from the app's name
branch: main                 # the branch that deploys when pushed

build:
  dockerfile: Dockerfile     # relative to the build context
  context: .                 # relative to the repository root
  args: {}                   # --build-arg values: not for secrets, they end up in image history

domains: [shop.example.com]  # in addition to the ones set with `domains set`

roles:
  web:
    port: 3000
    memory: 512M
    cpus: 1
    healthcheck: {path: /up, timeout: 5s, start_period: 60s}
    smoke: [/, /pricing]
    stop_timeout: 30s
  worker:
    cmd: worker
    memory: 256M

release_command: migrate up
services:
  postgres: true
  redis: false
watch:
  window: 3m
  error_rate: 2%
  min_requests: 20
  max_restarts: 2
keep_releases: 5
notify: [https://hooks.slack.com/services/...]
```

### Keys

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `app` | the app's name | Informational. |
| `branch` | `main` | Pushing this branch deploys. Overrides the branch chosen at `apps create`. |
| `build.dockerfile` | `Dockerfile` | Path of the Dockerfile, relative to the context. |
| `build.context` | `.` | Directory sent to `docker build`, relative to the repository root. Must stay inside the repository. |
| `build.args` | none | `--build-arg KEY=value`. Not for secrets. |
| `domains` | none | Domains served by the app. Combined with those set by `appdeploy domains set`. |
| `roles` | one `web` role | A map of role name to its settings. Names: lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `_`, starting with a letter. A role named `web` receives HTTP traffic. |
| `roles.<name>.on` | `[web]` | Server labels that run this role; only matters in a [group](groups.md). |
| `roles.<name>.port` | `EXPOSE` of the image, else `8080` | Port the app listens on. Passed to the app as `PORT`. Web role only. |
| `roles.<name>.cmd` | image's `CMD` | Replaces the image's `CMD` (arguments to its `ENTRYPOINT`). Quotes are respected, no shell is involved. |
| `roles.<name>.memory` | `512M` | Memory limit (`K`, `M`, `G`; at least `4M`). Swap is off. |
| `roles.<name>.cpus` | `1` | CPU limit. |
| `roles.<name>.replicas_per_server` | `1` | Containers of this role per server (1 to 32). |
| `roles.<name>.healthcheck.path` | `/up` | Web role. Must answer 2xx or 3xx. |
| `roles.<name>.healthcheck.timeout` | `5s` | Per request. |
| `roles.<name>.healthcheck.start_period` | `60s` | How long a new container has to become healthy. |
| `roles.<name>.smoke` | none | Extra paths (starting with `/`) that must answer below 500 before the switch. |
| `roles.<name>.stop_timeout` | `30s` | Time to finish in-flight work after `SIGTERM` before the container is killed. |
| `host` | none | Client side only: the server (`user@host`) that commands run on when you are in this directory and give no `--host`. The agent ignores it. |
| `hosts` | none | Client side only: named servers, `name: user@host`, for `--host NAME`. See [Choosing the server](commands.md#choosing-the-server). |
| `env` | none | A map of non-secret environment variables for every container, kept in git. Names are letters, digits and `_`; `PORT` and `APPDEPLOY_*` are reserved; values are single-line. Secrets with the same name win. Do not put secrets here: `appdeploy check` warns about names that look like one. |
| `roles.<name>.volumes` | none | Named volumes to mount, as `name:/absolute/path[:ro]`. The name is lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `_`; host directories are not supported. The Docker volume is `ad-<app>-<name>` (with the default `--instance`), is created on the first deploy, is shared by every release and is never removed by a deploy. Not backed up by appdeploy. |
| `release_command` | none | Run once per deploy before traffic moves, in a throwaway container of the new image with the release's environment. Like `cmd` it replaces the image's `CMD`. A failure stops the deploy. |
| `services.postgres` | `false` | A database for this app on the server's shared Postgres; provides `DATABASE_URL`. |
| `services.redis` | `false` | A Redis database number on the shared Redis; provides `REDIS_URL`. |
| `watch.window` | `3m` | How long the new release is watched after the switch. |
| `watch.error_rate` | `2%` | Roll back above this share of 5xx answers (or twice the previous release's rate, if higher). |
| `watch.min_requests` | `20` | Fewer requests than this in the window are not judged by the error rate. |
| `watch.max_restarts` | `2` | Roll back when a container restarted this many times. |
| `keep_releases` | `5` | Releases (and their images) kept for rollback. |
| `allow_partial` | `false` | In a group, roll out to the reachable servers and let the others catch up, instead of stopping at an unreachable one. |
| `notify` | none | Webhook URLs for this app's events (see [Operations](operations.md#notifications)). |

Roles other than `web` have no health check; they pass `verifying` if they are still running a
few seconds after start.

### The environment of your containers

Every container gets the `env` section of `appdeploy.yml`, then the app's secrets (a secret overrides an `env` entry of the same name), plus:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `PORT` | the web role's port (web role only) |
| `APPDEPLOY_APP`, `APPDEPLOY_RELEASE`, `APPDEPLOY_ROLE` | the app, the release number, the role name |
| `APPDEPLOY_SERVER` | the server's name (in a group) |
| `DATABASE_URL`, `REDIS_URL` | when `services` asks for them (a secret of the same name wins) |

### Volumes

A volume keeps files across deploys, rollbacks and restarts. Only **named volumes** are supported.
Things to know:

- During a deploy the old and the new container run at the same time, and both have the volume until
  the old one stops, after `watch.window` (3 minutes by default). Files that must have one writer,
  such as a SQLite database, are used by two processes meanwhile. SQLite copes with that in WAL mode,
  but you may set `watch.window` lower. The deploy log prints a warning, and `appdeploy check`
  warns when `replicas_per_server` is above 1 on a writable volume.
- If the image declares `VOLUME /data` and the role does not mount something there, the deploy is
  refused: Docker would use an anonymous volume that is deleted with the container.
- `appdeploy apps destroy` keeps the volumes (use `--delete-volumes` to remove them).
- Volumes live on one server. In a group, each server has its own copy of the data.

## Agent flags

Set on the `appdeploy agent` command line; for the installed service, edit `ExecStart` in
`/etc/systemd/system/appdeployd.service` and `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart appdeployd`.
The install script sets the ones it needs.

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--data-dir` | `/var/lib/appdeploy` | State directory. |
| `--socket` | `/run/appdeploy/agent.sock` | Control socket. |
| `--socket-group` | none (root only) | Group allowed to use the socket (the install script uses `appdeploy`). |
| `--repo-owner` | none | Unix user that owns app git repositories: the SSH user (`deploy`). |
| `--instance` | `ad` | Prefix of Docker names, so several agents can share one Docker (tests). |
| `--caddy-admin` | `http://127.0.0.1:2019` | Caddy's admin API, or `none` to run without a proxy. |
| `--caddy-listen` | `:443` | Where Caddy serves apps. |
| `--caddy-admin-listen` | none | Re-declare Caddy's admin address in the config it is given (needed when Caddy runs in a container). |
| `--no-tls` | off | Plain HTTP only (testing). |
| `--upstream-host` | `127.0.0.1` | Host the proxy uses to reach containers. |
| `--access-log` | none | Caddy's access log, read by the watchdog. Without it the watchdog only sees restarts and health. |
| `--caddy-access-log` | same as `--access-log` | The log's path as Caddy sees it, if different. |
| `--default-watch-window` | `3m` | `watch.window` for apps that do not set it. |
| `--min-free-bytes` | 5 GiB | Refuse to build with less free disk. |
| `--min-free-frac` | `0.10` | Refuse to build below this free fraction; also the `disk.low` alert threshold. |
| `--monitor-every` | `30s` | How often to look for crashed containers and low disk (0 = never). |
| `--notify-url` | none | A webhook for every app's events (repeatable). |
| `--backup-every` | `24h` | Postgres backups of all apps that use it (0 = never). |
| `--prune-build-cache` | off | After each deploy remove Docker build cache unused for this long (e.g. `168h`). Off because the cache is shared with everything else on that Docker. |
| `--network-pool` | Docker's default | CIDR to carve /24 networks for apps from (e.g. `172.80.0.0/12`). Docker's default pool holds only ~30 networks. |
| `--health-listen` | off | Address for `GET /health/<app>`, for load balancers. |
| `--peer-listen` | the advertised port | Address of the server-to-server API in a group. |
| `--update-repo` | `merkushin/appdeploy` | GitHub repository releases come from. |
| `--update-api` | GitHub's API | API URL for self-update (tests). |
| `--update-check-every` | `1m` | How often a group member checks whether it is its turn to install the group's wanted version (0 = never). |
| `--update-confirm-after` | `1m` | How long a freshly updated agent must stay healthy to count the update as good. |

## Files on disk

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `/usr/local/bin/appdeploy` | the binary; `appdeploy.previous` after an update, `appdeploy.failed` after a revert |
| `/var/lib/appdeploy/state.db` | apps, releases, deploy journal (SQLite) |
| `/var/lib/appdeploy/apps/<app>/repo.git` | the app's git repository |
| `/var/lib/appdeploy/apps/<app>/releases/` | the frozen secrets of each release (mode 0600) |
| `/var/lib/appdeploy/secrets/<app>.env` | the app's current secrets (mode 0600) |
| `/var/lib/appdeploy/services/` | generated Postgres and Redis credentials |
| `/var/lib/appdeploy/backups/<app>/` | database backups |
| `/var/lib/appdeploy/group/` | the group's CA, this server's certificate and the member list |
| `/var/lib/appdeploy/update-pending.json`, `update-failed.json` | update bookkeeping (see [Operations](operations.md#updating-appdeploy)) |
| `/var/lib/appdeploy/caddy/` | Caddy's certificates and saved config |
| `/var/log/appdeploy/access.log` | Caddy's JSON access log (rotated, 3 x 20 MB) |
| `/home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys` | who may use appdeploy, with their role |

---

<!-- file: docs/api.md -->

# HTTP API

The agent serves a JSON API over a **unix socket** (default `/run/appdeploy/agent.sock`). The
CLI is a client of it. Access is by file permission on the socket: root, plus the socket group if
configured. There is no other authentication, and **no TCP listener** for it.

```bash
curl -s --unix-socket /run/appdeploy/agent.sock http://agent/v1/apps
```

Errors are `{"error":"message"}` with status 400 (404 if not found). The API is not versioned
beyond the `/v1` prefix and may change before 1.0; the CLI is the stable interface.

Times are RFC 3339. A deploy's `state` is one of `queued`, `validating`, `building`, `migrating`,
`starting`, `verifying`, `switching`, `observing`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `rolled_back`,
`superseded` (and `distributing`, `rolling` for a coordinator in a group).

## Apps

| Request | Body | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /v1/ping` | | `{"ok":true}` |
| `POST /v1/apps` | `{"name","domains":[],"branch"}` | 201, the app: `{"name","domains","branch","current_release","created_at"}` |
| `GET /v1/apps` | | list of apps |
| `GET /v1/apps/{app}` | | `{"app":{...},"containers":[{"name","role","release","running","restarts","host_port"}],"deploys":[{"id","app","release","state","error","ref","source","started_at","finished_at"}],"releases":[{"number","commit","image","created_at","current"}]}` |
| `DELETE /v1/apps/{app}` | query `volumes=1` also deletes the volumes | `{"ok":true,"kept_volumes":[...]}` (destructive) |
| `PUT /v1/apps/{app}/domains` | `{"domains":[]}` | `{"ok":true}` |
| `GET /v1/apps/{app}/releases` | | list of releases |
| `GET /v1/apps/{app}/export?format=kamal` | | `{"files":{"path":"content"}}` |

## Deploying

Each of these answers `202 {"deploy_id":"..."}` and returns at once; follow the deploy with the
events endpoint.

| Request | Body |
|---|---|
| `POST /v1/apps/{app}/deploy` | `{"ref":"sha-or-ref"}` or `{"image":"ref","config_yaml":"..."}` |
| `POST /v1/apps/{app}/redeploy` | none |
| `POST /v1/apps/{app}/rollback` | `{"to":N}` (0 or absent: the previous release) |
| `POST /v1/apps/{app}/push` | `{"ref":"refs/heads/main","sha":"..."}`; called by the git hook; answers 200 `{"message"}` if the ref is not the deploy branch |
| `GET /v1/deploys/{id}` | the deploy, as above |
| `GET /v1/deploys/{id}/events?after=N` | newline-delimited JSON: `{"id","time","msg"}` for each journal line, ending with `{"done":true,"state","error"}` |

The `time` field is absent on the last line. The events stream is how to wait: read until a line with `"done":true` and check `state`
(`succeeded` is success). Reconnect with `after=<last id>` if the connection drops; the deploy
does not depend on it.

## Secrets, logs, commands

| Request | Body | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /v1/apps/{app}/secrets` | | `{"names":[...]}` |
| `GET /v1/apps/{app}/secrets?reveal=1` | | `{"values":{"KEY":"value"}}` (secret values) |
| `POST /v1/apps/{app}/secrets` | `{"set":{"K":"v"},"unset":["K"],"deploy":true}` | `{"deploy_id"}` if `deploy` and the app has a release |
| `GET /v1/apps/{app}/logs?role=web&follow=1&tail=100` | | text, lines prefixed with the container name |
| `POST /v1/apps/{app}/exec` | `{"role":"web","cmd":["ls","/"]}` | the output as a stream; the exit status is in the HTTP trailer `Appdeploy-Exit` |

## Databases

| Request | Body | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /v1/apps/{app}/db/backup` | | `{"path"}` |
| `GET /v1/apps/{app}/db/backups` | | `["name",...]`, newest first |
| `POST /v1/apps/{app}/db/restore` | `{"file":"name"}` | `{"ok":true}`; replaces the database's tables |

## Group and updates

| Request | Body | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /v1/group` | | members and wanted version; 400 if not in a group |
| `GET /v1/group/versions` | | `{"desired","servers":[{"name","addr","labels","version","reachable","busy","error"}]}` |
| `POST /v1/group/invite` | | `{"token"}` (founder) |
| `POST /v1/group/version` | `{"version":"v1.2.3"}` or `""` | the group state (founder) |
| `DELETE /v1/group/servers/{name}` | | the group state (founder) |
| `POST /v1/self-update` | `{"check":false,"force":false,"repo":""}` | `{"log":[...],"from","to","updated","error"}`; after `updated`, the agent restarts in a second |

## Health endpoint

With `--health-listen`, a separate TCP listener answers `GET /health/{app}` with 200 `ok` when this
server runs a web container of the app's live release, else 503 (`not serving`, or `switching`
while traffic is being moved). Nothing else, and no authentication, for load balancers.

## Peer API (between servers)

Served over mutual TLS on the peer port; not for you to call. It is listed so that you know what
a group exposes: `POST /peer/v1/join`, `GET /peer/v1/ping`, `GET /peer/v1/version`,
`GET /peer/v1/group`, `PUT /peer/v1/group`, `POST /peer/v1/image`, `GET /peer/v1/image`,
`POST /peer/v1/source`, `POST /peer/v1/deploy`, `GET /peer/v1/deploys/{id}/events`,
`GET /peer/v1/finals`, `PUT /peer/v1/final`, `GET /peer/v1/release`.

---

<!-- file: docs/groups.md -->

# Server groups

A **group** is a few servers (1 to about 10) that deploy together. Use one when you want an app
or its worker on several machines, a separate build server, or to run different roles of one
app on different servers. A single server needs no group.

## How it works

- Every server has a name and **labels** (`web`, `db`, `worker`, `builder`, anything you like).
- A role runs on the servers whose labels match its `on:` list (default `[web]`).
- The first server creates the group and is its **founder**; it holds the group's private
  certificate authority. Others join with a one-hour, single-use invite token. All
  server-to-server traffic is TLS 1.3 with certificates from that authority on both sides.
- You deploy as usual by pushing to **one** server (the app's git repository lives only there:
  always push to the same one). That server is the **coordinator** of the deploy.

A deploy in a group:

1. The coordinator checks out the commit and builds the image **once** (on a server with the
   label `builder` if there is one), runs `release_command` once, and sends the image to the
   other servers directly (no registry).
2. It rolls out in **waves**: up to 3 target servers one at a time; with more, a canary first and
   then 25% at a time. Each server runs the normal sequence (start, verify, switch, observe). The
   canary is watched for at most a minute, later waves for at most 20 seconds, instead of the
   full `watch.window`.
3. If a server fails in a later wave, the servers that already switched are **taken back** to
   their previous release and the deploy fails with `rollout stopped in wave N`.
4. Rollback (`appdeploy rollback`) goes back on every server.

Each server routes only to its own containers: spread traffic across servers with a load
balancer or DNS in front. Each server answers `GET /health/<app>` (enable it with
`--health-listen`) with 200 when it runs the app and 503 otherwise, including for the moment
traffic is being switched.

## Set up a group

You need each server to be able to reach the others on the **peer port** (the port in
`--advertise`, e.g. 7070); nothing else is exposed between them. Install appdeploy on every
server first ([Getting started](getting-started.md)).

**1. Create the group on the first server (the founder):**

```bash
ssh root@a systemctl stop appdeployd
ssh root@a appdeploy group init --server a --advertise a.internal:7070 --labels web,db --group prod
ssh root@a systemctl start appdeployd
```

`--advertise` is the address other servers use to reach this one. The certificate is issued for
that host name or IP, so use the same name later.

**2. Invite a server** (from your computer; admin):

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@a group invite
```

It prints the command to run on the new server.

**3. On the new server**, after installing appdeploy, run it **before the agent runs**:

```bash
ssh root@b systemctl stop appdeployd
ssh root@b appdeploy group join --server b --advertise b.internal:7070 --labels web --token <token>
ssh root@b systemctl start appdeployd
```

**4. Look at the result:**

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@a group servers
```
```
SERVER  ADDRESS            LABELS    VERSION  STATE
a       a.internal:7070    web,db    0.1.1    ok
b       b.internal:7070    web       0.1.1    ok
```

The member list is replicated: every server learns of changes within seconds, and a server that
was down learns when it returns. `group remove <name>` (on the founder) drops a server.

Back up `/var/lib/appdeploy/group/` on the founder: it holds the authority's key. Without it you
cannot add servers; there is no key rotation yet. Everything else keeps working.

## Using labels

```yaml appdeploy.yml
roles:
  web:
    on: [web]            # on every server labeled web
    replicas_per_server: 2
  worker:
    on: [worker]
    cmd: worker
release_command: migrate
```

- A server runs only the roles whose labels match. A server with none of an app's labels does
  nothing for it (it can still be the coordinator or the builder).
- Domains are served by every server that runs the `web` role; put DNS or a balancer in front.
  Servers learn an app's domains when they deploy it: after `domains set` on the coordinator,
  run `appdeploy redeploy` so the others get them too.
- `release_command` runs once, on the coordinator, before any server switches.
- `services:` (Postgres, Redis) are only available when every role of the app runs on the
  coordinating server. For an app spread over servers use an external database through a
  `DATABASE_URL` secret.

## Build servers

A server with the label `builder` builds for the group: the coordinator sends it the source,
it builds under its own build slot and disk check, and the coordinator fetches the image. It
removes its copy afterwards. With several, the first by name is used. If the coordinator is
itself a builder, it builds locally. Give a builder a lot of RAM and disk and no app roles.

## When a server is down

By default a deploy stops with `server X is not reachable` before anything changes. With
`allow_partial: true` the reachable servers get the release and the missing one is skipped with
a warning. When it returns (or joins later), it **catches up by itself**: the coordinator records
the release a completed rollout left the group on, servers exchange these records, and a server
that is not on that release fetches it from a peer and runs its part. It does nothing while a
deploy of that app is running on it, and it never moves an app back if something newer
succeeded there since.

A server that speaks a different peer **protocol** (only during an update of the group) refuses
the deploy until all servers run compatible versions.

## Updating all servers

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@a group set-version v0.2.0
```

Every server installs that release itself, one at a time in name order, waiting while anything
is being deployed, and reverts automatically if the new version does not stay up. Watch it with
`group servers`. Details: [Operations: updating](operations.md#updating-appdeploy).

## Limits

- 1 to about 10 servers. There is no scheduler: you place roles with labels.
- The founder is needed to add or remove servers, not to deploy.
- Every member can call every other member's peer API; there are no per-server permissions.
- No load balancer is provided.

---

<!-- file: docs/operations.md -->

# Operations

## Deploying from CI

`git push` exits with status 0 even if the deploy fails (git ignores what the hook reports after
it accepted the push), so a CI job cannot rely on it. Three ways that do work:

**Push to a branch that does not deploy, then deploy by commit.** `deploy` waits and exits
non-zero if the deploy did not succeed:

```bash
git push deploy@my-server:myapp HEAD:refs/heads/ci        # not the deploy branch: nothing happens
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server deploy myapp --ref "$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
```

**Build the image in CI** and have the server pull it. Log the server in to your registry once
(`docker login`), then:

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server deploy myapp --image registry.example.com/myapp:$GIT_SHA --config - < appdeploy.yml
```

(`--config` names a file on the machine where the command *runs*, which over `--host` is the server;
`--config -` reads it from standard input, so it travels from CI. Leave `--config` out to reuse the
live release's config.)

**Read the push output** for the line `==> succeeded` (and fail if you see `deploy failed`).

Give CI a key with the `deployer` role: it can deploy and roll back, but not read secrets,
run commands in containers or destroy anything.

## Looking at things

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server status myapp
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server logs myapp -f
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server releases myapp
```

On the server: `systemctl status appdeployd appdeploy-caddy`, `journalctl -u appdeployd`,
`journalctl -u appdeploy-caddy`, `docker ps`. The agent's journal of each deploy is what you
see during the deploy; the last ones are in `status`.

## Secrets

Secrets are the app's environment variables. `secrets set` stores them (mode 0600, readable by
root only) and makes a new release without rebuilding. A release keeps a frozen copy, so
a rollback restores the old values. `secrets list` shows names only; `secrets export` prints
values (admin) and is the way to take them with you.

To change several at once without restarting the app several times, use `--no-deploy` for all
but the last, or all with `--no-deploy` and then `appdeploy redeploy`.

## Domains and HTTPS

`appdeploy domains set myapp a.example.com www.a.example.com` takes effect immediately. Caddy
requests a Let's Encrypt certificate on the first request, so DNS must already point at the
server and ports 80 and 443 must be open. Unknown host names get a plain `404 no such app`.

## Databases and backups

`services: {postgres: true}` gives the app its own database and role on a Postgres container
that appdeploy runs for you (`postgres:17-alpine`, data in a Docker volume), and `DATABASE_URL`
in its environment. The password is generated once and kept across deploys. Redis works the same
(`REDIS_URL`, a Redis database number per app, up to 15 apps; the numbers separate keys, they
are not a security boundary).

Backups: every `--backup-every` (24h) the agent writes a gzip `pg_dump` per app to
`/var/lib/appdeploy/backups/<app>/`, keeping the newest of each of the last 7 days and 4 weeks.
`appdeploy db backup <app>` takes one now; `db list` lists; `db restore <app> <name>` replaces the
database's tables with the backup. **Backups live on the same disk as the data**: copy them off the
server, for example with a nightly job on another machine:

```bash
rsync -a --delete root@my-server:/var/lib/appdeploy/backups/ /backups/appdeploy/
```

`apps destroy` keeps an app's database and backups on purpose, and its volumes too (`--delete-volumes`
removes them). **Volumes are not backed up**: copy them off the server, for example with
`docker run --rm -v ad-APP-NAME:/from:ro -v $PWD:/to alpine tar -C /from -czf /to/APP-NAME.tgz .`.

## Notifications

Webhooks receive deploy events from `notify:` in `appdeploy.yml` (per app) and from the agent's
`--notify-url` (all apps). Slack incoming webhooks and the Telegram Bot API get a text line;
anything else gets JSON:

```json
{"event":"deploy.rolled_back","app":"shop","release":3,"deploy_id":"1a1d9518857872f3fbe1d",
 "state":"rolled_back","commit":"75965914bef2f8d4b6ad882017382889b3e34f04",
 "error":"3 of 40 requests (7.5%) failed with 5xx, above the 2.0% limit","time":"2026-11-14T09:09:21Z"}
```

| Event | When |
|---|---|
| `deploy.started` | A deploy began (after its config was read). |
| `deploy.succeeded` | The release is live and its watch window passed. |
| `deploy.failed` | The deploy failed before traffic moved; the old release still serves. |
| `deploy.rolled_back` | The watchdog moved traffic back. `error` says why. |
| `migration.suspect` | The old release started failing right after `release_command`. |
| `app.crashed` | A container was restarted by Docker, stopped, or is restarting repeatedly. Once per incident, at most every 10 minutes per container. |
| `disk.low` | Free space on the data disk fell below the build threshold. Once until it recovers. |
| `backup.failed` | The scheduled database backup failed. |
| `agent.update_failed` | An update of the agent was reverted. |

Delivery is retried twice for transient errors, not for 4xx answers. URLs are never written to
logs because they carry secrets.

## Security

- **Ports.** 22, 80 and 443 face the world. In a group, the peer port is used between servers
  only; the health port (`--health-listen`) answers a bare status. The install script does not
  touch the firewall: do it yourself.
- **SSH.** The user `deploy` can run nothing but appdeploy: the key's `authorized_keys` line forces
  the command `appdeploy shell --role <role>`, which accepts git push/fetch of an existing app and
  appdeploy commands, and nothing else; options such as `--host` or `--socket` from the client are
  refused. Roles: `admin` (everything; keys given with `--ssh-key`), `deployer` (push, deploy,
  redeploy, rollback, logs, secret names), `viewer` (status and lists). Anyone who can run `exec`
  or `secrets export` (admin) can read every secret.
- **The agent runs as root** and controls Docker, so whoever controls the agent controls the server.
  The control socket is accessible to root and, if configured, one group.
- **Containers** run with the user your image sets (use a non-root `USER`), have memory and CPU
  limits, no extra privileges, no access to the Docker socket, and a network of their own per app.
  They publish their port on `127.0.0.1` only.
- **Secrets** are files with mode 0600 and are put into containers as environment variables. They
  are not in build arguments, logs or the push output. Values passed to `secrets set` are visible in
  your shell history and process list.
- **Group traffic** is mutually authenticated TLS 1.3 with a private authority, joined with
  single-use tokens that pin the authority's fingerprint.
- **Updates** are verified with a signature before they are installed; the key is built into the
  binary.

## Updating appdeploy

Releases are published on GitHub, signed with a key whose public half is built into every binary
(`appdeploy version --verbose` shows it and its fingerprint, which the release notes repeat).
Each binary also has a build attestation: `gh attestation verify <file> --repo merkushin/appdeploy`.

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server self-update --check     # is there a newer release
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server self-update             # install it
```

The agent downloads the release, verifies the signature and the checksum, runs the new binary
once, keeps the old one as `/usr/local/bin/appdeploy.previous`, replaces the binary and restarts
(the service manager starts the new one). Your apps keep running; a deploy in progress resumes. It
refuses while deploys are running unless you pass `--force`.

**A bad update reverts itself.** Before each start the service runs `appdeploy recover`. If a
freshly installed version does not manage to stay up (it is confirmed after being healthy for a
minute), the fourth start puts `appdeploy.previous` back, keeps the bad binary as
`appdeploy.failed`, and the agent sends `agent.update_failed`. A version that failed is not tried
again until another is asked for. This needs the `ExecStartPre` line and
`StartLimitIntervalSec=0` that the install script writes, so run the script again on servers
installed earlier.

**A whole group** updates from one command on the founder:

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@a group set-version v0.2.0
appdeploy --host deploy@a group servers          # watch the versions change, in name order
```

To go back by hand: `mv /usr/local/bin/appdeploy.previous /usr/local/bin/appdeploy` and
`systemctl restart appdeployd`.

## Disk

Old releases beyond `keep_releases` are removed with their images after each deploy, dangling
images of appdeploy's builds too. Docker's build cache and images unrelated to appdeploy are not
touched unless you pass `--prune-build-cache`. Docker's disk use is shown by `docker system df`.
Builds are refused when free disk is below 5 GiB or 10% (`disk.low` is sent at the same
threshold); the thresholds are agent flags.

## Uninstalling

This deletes all apps' state; export what you need first (see [Migration](migration.md)).

```bash
# containers and networks of appdeploy (they are labelled appdeploy.instance)
docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq --filter label=appdeploy.instance)
docker network rm $(docker network ls -q --filter label=appdeploy.instance)
systemctl disable --now appdeployd appdeploy-caddy
rm /etc/systemd/system/appdeployd.service /etc/systemd/system/appdeploy-caddy.service
rm -r /var/lib/appdeploy /etc/appdeploy /usr/local/bin/appdeploy*
userdel -r deploy
```

Docker volumes of Postgres and Redis (`ad-svc-*`) remain: `docker volume rm` them if you want the
data gone.

---

<!-- file: docs/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

Start with these, on your computer and on the server:

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server status myapp          # what runs, and how the last deploys ended
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server logs myapp --tail 50
ssh root@my-server systemctl status appdeployd appdeploy-caddy
ssh root@my-server journalctl -u appdeployd -n 100 --no-pager
```

A deploy that fails **before traffic moved** (`failed`) leaves the old release serving and cleans
up after itself, so a failure is usually not an outage. The error message is the last `deploy failed:`
line of the output.

## The deploy fails

| Message (part of it) | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `healthcheck GET /up did not pass within 1m0s` | The new container never answered 2xx/3xx on that path. The last lines of its log are printed above. | Check the app listens on `$PORT` on all interfaces, serves `/up` (or set `roles.web.healthcheck.path`), and starts within `start_period`. |
| `... exited (code 1)` / `exited right after starting` | The container crashed. Its last log lines are printed. | Fix the crash; reproduce with `docker run` locally using the same environment variables. `killed for exceeding its memory limit` means raise `roles.<name>.memory`. |
| `build failed: ...` | `docker build` failed; the end of its output is in the message and the full output above it. | Fix the Dockerfile; the build ran on the server, so base images must be reachable from it. |
| `Dockerfile not found in the repository (build.dockerfile)` | No file at `build.dockerfile` inside `build.context`. | Check the paths in `appdeploy.yml`; they are relative to the context, which is relative to the repository root. |
| `release command failed` | `release_command` exited non-zero, so nothing started. Its output is above. | Fix the migration. Nothing changed for users. |
| `not enough memory: ... already reserved by running containers + ... needed > ...` | The memory limits of all containers on the server, including the new release's and the old one still running, do not fit in RAM minus a reserve (15% or 512 MB). | Lower limits, remove apps, or use a bigger server. Remember both releases run at once during a deploy. |
| `not enough disk space to build` | Free disk is below 5 GiB or 10%. | Free space (`docker system df`, `docker image prune`) or lower the thresholds (`--min-free-bytes`, `--min-free-frac`). |
| `appdeploy.yml: ... field xyz not found` | An unknown key, usually a typo. | Fix it; keys are listed in [Configuration](configuration.md). |
| `invalid duration "..."` / `invalid size "..."` | A value is wrong. | Use `5s`, `3m`, `512M`, `1G`. |
| `git ref "..." not found in the app repository` | `deploy --ref X` with a commit the server does not have. | Push it first (to a branch that does not deploy). |
| `superseded by ...` | A newer deploy of the same app replaced this one while it waited. | Nothing: the newer one runs. |
| `gave up after N attempts interrupted by agent restarts` | The agent kept restarting during this deploy. | Look at `journalctl -u appdeployd`; deploy again. |
| `pulling X: ... (private registries need docker login on the server)` | `deploy --image` could not pull it. | `docker login` on the server for a private registry; check the name and tag. |
| `invalid image reference` | The `--image` value has unexpected characters. | Use `registry/name:tag`. |

## The deploy succeeded, then rolled back

State `rolled_back`; the last lines say `watchdog: ...`:

| Message | Cause |
|---|---|
| `N of M requests (x%) failed with 5xx, above the y% limit` | The new version returned errors under real traffic. Look at its logs (`logs` shows the live release only, so read the journal above or reproduce), fix, deploy again. |
| `... restarted N times` / `... exited` | A container crashed after it passed the checks (a crash loop, memory limit). |
| `health check GET /up failed 3 times in a row` | The app stopped answering after the switch. |

Raise `watch.error_rate` or lower `watch.min_requests` only if the thresholds do not suit your
traffic. A single failed request does not trigger anything.

## Commands

| Message | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `cannot reach the agent at /run/appdeploy/agent.sock` | The agent is not running (`systemctl status appdeployd`) or you cannot use the socket (it is root's, or a group's, see `--socket-group`). Over SSH this appears on the server's side. |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` | Your key is not in `/home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys`; run `install.sh` again with `--ssh-key-file` / `--deployer-key` / `--viewer-key`. |
| `"deploy" is not allowed for the viewer role` | Your key's role is too low; see [Operations: security](operations.md#security). |
| `interactive shells are not available` | You ran `ssh deploy@server` without a command. Use `appdeploy --host ...`. |
| `unexpected option "--host"` | You passed a client option inside an SSH command. |
| `no such app "x" (create it with: appdeploy apps create x)` | `git push` to an app that does not exist. |
| `app "x" already exists` | `apps create` of an existing name. |
| `... is not the deploy branch (main): not deploying` | You pushed another branch. That is by design. |
| `release vN of x not found (it may have been pruned)` | `rollback --to N` of a release beyond `keep_releases`. |
| `there is no earlier release to roll back to` | Only one release exists. |
| `vN is already the current release` | `rollback --to N` of the live release. |
| `app "x" has nothing deployed yet` | `redeploy` before the first deploy. |
| `app "x" has a deploy in progress` (apps destroy) | Wait for it. |
| `the image declares VOLUME` | The Dockerfile has `VOLUME /path` and the role mounts nothing there; Docker would lose the data at the next deploy. Add `roles.<name>.volumes: ["data:/path"]` or remove `VOLUME`. |
| `docker is not reachable` (agent start) | Docker is not running: `systemctl status docker`. |

## HTTPS and domains

- **No certificate / browser warning:** the domain must resolve to this server and ports 80 and 443
  must be reachable from the internet. Look at `journalctl -u appdeploy-caddy` for the
  Let's Encrypt error; wait out rate limits rather than retrying.
- **`404 no such app`:** the host name is not one of the app's domains (`appdeploy status myapp` shows
  them), or the app has no release yet.
- **`502`/connection errors right after a deploy:** check `status`; a container that is not `running`
  is the cause.

## Groups

| Message | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `server X is not reachable (...)` | The coordinator cannot reach X's peer port. Start it, fix the firewall, or set `allow_partial: true`. |
| `server X speaks protocol N and this one M` | The group is in the middle of an update. Wait until `group servers` shows one version. |
| `no server of the group carries the labels the roles ask for` | `roles.*.on` matches no server's labels. |
| `services (postgres/redis) are only available when every role runs on the coordinating server` | Use an external `DATABASE_URL` secret instead. |
| `rollout stopped in wave N` | A server failed in wave N; the ones before it were taken back. The line before says why. |
| `invalid or expired invite` | Tokens work once for one hour: run `group invite` again. |
| `the server's CA does not match the invite (wrong server?)` | You are joining a different group than the invite came from. |
| `only the server that created the group can ...` | `invite`, `remove` and `set-version` only work on the founder. |
| `waiting for X to update first` (agent log) | The group's update is going one server at a time; it is not stuck. A server that stays on the old version stops the ones behind it. |

## Updates

| Message | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `... has <repo> published a release?` | The GitHub repository has no release. |
| `the signature of SHA256SUMS is not valid ... refusing to install` | The release was not signed by the key built into this binary: do not install it. |
| `this binary was built without a release signing key` | A development build cannot verify updates; install a release binary. |
| `N deploy(s) are in progress` | Try again later, or `--force`. |
| `installing X failed here before and was reverted` (agent log) | A group member will not retry a version that failed on it; set another version. |

---

<!-- file: docs/migration.md -->

# Migration

There is an importer for Kamal (`appdeploy import kamal`); for other sources moving is a few
manual steps, listed here, and [leaving appdeploy](#leaving-appdeploy) is one command plus your data.

The model that makes moves cheap: your app is a **Dockerfile**, **environment variables** and
`GET /up`. Everything else (ports, domains, limits) is a few lines of
[`appdeploy.yml`](configuration.md).

## Before you move: check the fit

| If your app... | Then |
|---|---|
| writes files it must keep (uploads, SQLite) | Mount a named volume (`roles.<name>.volumes`) and copy the data in ([moving a volume](#moving-a-volume)). Volumes are not backed up by appdeploy; for important data prefer Postgres or object storage. |
| is built with buildpacks (Heroku, Dokku, Fly) and has no Dockerfile | Write a Dockerfile. appdeploy never guesses a build. |
| needs more than ~10 servers or autoscaling | Not what appdeploy is for. |
| has background workers or cron | Fine: extra roles (`cmd:`). Run schedules inside a worker process; there is no cron feature. |

A safe way to move any app: set it up on appdeploy **next to** the old deployment (a new server,
or another port), deploy, test with a temporary domain, move the data, then switch DNS.

## From Kamal

| Kamal (`config/deploy.yml`) | appdeploy |
|---|---|
| `service:` | the app name (`apps create <name>`) |
| `image:` and `registry:` | not needed: the server builds the image. To keep building in CI, `deploy --image` pulls from your registry (`docker login` on the server once). |
| `servers:` `web:` hosts | servers labeled `web` (one server needs no labels) |
| `servers:` other roles (`job:` with `cmd:`) | `roles.<name>` with `cmd:` and `on: [label]` |
| `proxy: host / hosts, ssl` | `domains:` (HTTPS is automatic) |
| `proxy: app_port` | `roles.web.port` |
| `proxy: healthcheck: path` | `roles.web.healthcheck.path` |
| `env: clear:` | the `env:` section of `appdeploy.yml` |
| `env: secret:` and `.kamal/secrets` | `appdeploy secrets set <app> NAME=value...` |
| `accessories:` postgres / redis | `services: {postgres: true}` (a database per app, backups) or keep your own and set `DATABASE_URL` |
| `accessories:` anything else | run it yourself next to appdeploy, or keep it on Kamal |
| `volumes:` (named) | `roles.<name>.volumes` (see [moving a volume](#moving-a-volume)); a host directory is not supported |
| `hooks/pre-deploy` (migrations) | `release_command:` |
| `builder:` options | not needed (build happens on the server) |
| `kamal deploy` | `git push prod main` (or `appdeploy deploy`) |
| `kamal rollback <version>` | `appdeploy rollback <app> [--to N]` |
| `kamal app logs`, `kamal app exec` | `appdeploy logs`, `appdeploy exec` |

**Let the tool do the reading first.** In your project directory, on your computer:

```bash
appdeploy import kamal                 # reads config/deploy.yml and .kamal/secrets
appdeploy import kamal --out appdeploy.yml
```

It prints the `appdeploy.yml` for the app, the commands to create it and set its secrets, and
three lists: **blockers** (the app cannot run on appdeploy as it is: host directory mounts, accessories other
than Postgres and Redis), **not carried over**, and **things to decide**. It changes nothing on any
server and does not read secret values. Solve the blockers before you go on; the tables below explain
each mapping, and `appdeploy check appdeploy.yml` validates the result.

Steps: install appdeploy on a **new** server, create the app with its domain(s), `secrets set`
the values from `.kamal/secrets`, push, check with a test request (`curl --resolve
myapp.example.com:443:<new-ip> https://myapp.example.com/up`), copy the database
([below](#moving-a-postgres-database-in)), lower the DNS TTL, switch DNS, and keep Kamal running
until traffic has moved. To do it on the **same** server, Kamal's proxy and appdeploy's Caddy both
want ports 80 and 443: expect a short gap while you stop Kamal's proxy and start appdeploy's.

## From Docker Compose

| Compose | appdeploy |
|---|---|
| a service that serves HTTP | the `web` role; `ports:` becomes `domains:` and `roles.web.port` |
| other services running your image with another `command:` | roles with `cmd:` |
| `environment:`, `env_file:` | `env:` in `appdeploy.yml` for plain values, `secrets set` for secrets |
| `build:` | the Dockerfile (and `build.context`, `build.args`) |
| `mem_limit`, `cpus` | `roles.<name>.memory`, `.cpus` |
| `healthcheck:` | `roles.web.healthcheck` (an HTTP path, probed from outside) |
| `postgres`, `redis` services | `services:` (or keep them elsewhere with `DATABASE_URL`) |
| named `volumes:` for your app | `roles.<name>.volumes`; bind mounts are not supported |
| a reverse proxy service (Caddy, Traefik, nginx) | not needed: Caddy is built in |

Put the repository's Dockerfile at the root, write `appdeploy.yml` from the table, push.

## From Dokku or Heroku

| Dokku / Heroku | appdeploy |
|---|---|
| `git push dokku main` | `git push prod main` |
| buildpack (`heroku/nodejs`, ...) | a Dockerfile (required) |
| `Procfile` entries (`web:`, `worker:`) | roles: `web` runs the image's default `CMD`; others use `cmd:` |
| `release:` in the Procfile | `release_command:` |
| `config:set KEY=value` | `secrets set` |
| `domains:add` | `apps create --domain` / `domains set` |
| `ps:scale web=2` | `roles.web.replicas_per_server: 2` |
| `CHECKS` / health check settings | `roles.web.healthcheck` |
| `postgres:create`, `redis:create` plugins | `services:` |
| `storage:mount` | not supported |
| Let's Encrypt plugin | built in |

## From Fly.io, Render, Railway

| Hosted platform | appdeploy |
|---|---|
| `fly.toml` `[http_service] internal_port` | `roles.web.port` |
| `[[http_service.checks]] path` | `roles.web.healthcheck.path` |
| `[processes]` | roles (`cmd:`) |
| `[vm] memory` | `roles.<name>.memory` |
| `fly secrets set`, dashboard env vars | `secrets set` |
| `[mounts]` volumes | `roles.<name>.volumes` (copy the data in: [moving a volume](#moving-a-volume)) |
| managed Postgres | keep it and set `DATABASE_URL`, or `services: {postgres: true}` and restore a dump |
| `fly deploy` | `git push prod main` |
| certificates | automatic |

## Moving a volume

appdeploy creates the volume `ad-<app>-<name>` on the first deploy (`ad` is the agent's
`--instance`). Data from an old volume is copied into it **before the first deploy**, with the old
app stopped so nothing is written meanwhile. Create the new volume with the labels that make
`apps destroy` know it, copy, and check:

```bash
APP=myapp; NAME=data; OLD=myapp_data      # your app, the volume name in appdeploy.yml, the old volume
docker volume create --label appdeploy.instance=ad --label appdeploy.app=$APP --label appdeploy.volume=$NAME ad-$APP-$NAME
docker run --rm -v $OLD:/from:ro -v ad-$APP-$NAME:/to alpine cp -a /from/. /to/
docker run --rm -v ad-$APP-$NAME:/v:ro alpine ls -la /v
```

For a SQLite database, stop the old app first (or copy with `sqlite3 old.db ".backup new.db"`) so
that the copy is consistent. For the files of a host directory, mount it as `/from` instead of the volume.

## Moving a Postgres database in

Take a plain SQL dump from the old database that does not depend on its users:

```bash
pg_dump --clean --if-exists --no-owner --no-acl "$OLD_DATABASE_URL" | gzip > import.sql.gz
```

With `services: {postgres: true}` deployed once (so the app's database exists), copy the dump into
the app's backup directory on the server and restore it:

```bash
ssh root@my-server mkdir -p /var/lib/appdeploy/backups/myapp
scp import.sql.gz root@my-server:/var/lib/appdeploy/backups/myapp/
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server db restore myapp import.sql.gz
```

`restore` replaces the tables of the app's database with the dump's, so do it once, before you
switch traffic (or put the app in a quiet state first). The dump is a plain SQL file replayed
with `psql`; appdeploy's own backups are exactly that format, which is what has been tested.
Stop writes to the old database and take a final dump right before the cutover.

## Leaving appdeploy

Everything appdeploy knows can be written for another tool, and nothing appdeploy-specific is
inside your image or code.

**1. Generate the target's files**, from the live app:

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server export myapp --format kamal   --out ./deploy-kamal
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server export myapp --format compose --out ./deploy-compose
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server export myapp --format k8s     --out ./deploy-k8s
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server export myapp --format fly     --out ./deploy-fly
```

You get roles, ports, limits, health path, domains and the **names** of secrets, with notes where
you need to decide something (a registry name, the database). Values are never in these files.

| Format | Files | Maps |
|---|---|---|
| `kamal` | `config/deploy.yml`, `.kamal/secrets` | roles to Kamal roles with your servers by label, domains to `proxy`, Postgres/Redis to accessories |
| `compose` | `compose.yml`, `.env.example`, `Caddyfile` | a service per role with limits, Postgres/Redis services, Caddy for the domains |
| `k8s` | `k8s.yml` | a Secret template, a Deployment per role, a Service and an Ingress |
| `fly` | `fly.toml`, `secrets.sh` | processes, health check, VM size, a script that sets the secrets |

**2. Get the image into a registry.** appdeploy builds images on the servers and does not push
them. The image of release N is `ad/<app>:vN` on the server. Either build from your repository in
the new system, or push what is running:

```bash
ssh root@my-server
docker tag ad/myapp:v7 registry.example.com/myapp:v7
docker push registry.example.com/myapp:v7
```

The exported files use the placeholder `your-registry.example.com/myapp:vN`; replace it.

**3. Take your secrets and your data:**

```bash
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server secrets export myapp > myapp.env      # contains values: protect it
appdeploy --host deploy@my-server db backup myapp                        # then copy it off the server
scp root@my-server:/var/lib/appdeploy/backups/myapp/<name>.sql.gz .
gunzip -c <name>.sql.gz | psql "$NEW_DATABASE_URL"
```

Redis data is not backed up by appdeploy; if you use it for more than a cache, take a dump from
the Redis container yourself.

**4. Take the source:** the repository on the server is an ordinary bare git repository:
`git clone deploy@my-server:myapp` works, and `git remote` on your side is all you need.

**5. Switch DNS** once the new system serves the app, then run `appdeploy apps destroy myapp`
(keeping the database until you are sure) and [uninstall](operations.md#uninstalling).

**What does not carry over:** deploy history and the journal, TLS certificates (the new system
requests its own), and the contents of your app's volumes: `appdeploy export` writes the volume
mounts into the new tool's file, but you copy the data yourself (`docker run --rm -v ad-APP-NAME:/from:ro
-v $PWD:/to alpine tar -C /from -cf /to/data.tar .` makes an archive).

---

<!-- file: docs/comparison.md -->

# Comparison: when to choose appdeploy

appdeploy is for people who run **a handful of web apps on one to ten servers they control** and
want deploys that are boring: `git push`, a safe switch, an automatic way back. Below, how it
differs from the tools you are likely to be weighing. We describe the other tools as we
understand them at the time of writing; check their documentation before deciding.

## The short version

| | appdeploy | Kamal | Dokku | Coolify / Dokploy | Fly.io, Render, Railway | Compose + SSH scripts | Kubernetes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Who drives a deploy | agent on the server | your machine or CI, over SSH | server (git hook) | server, via web UI | their platform | your script | the cluster |
| Survives your connection dropping mid-deploy | yes, and resumes after crashes | the client drives it, so no | server-side, but check | yes | yes | no | yes |
| Needs a container registry | no | yes (can be a local one) | no | optional | built in | optional | yes |
| Automatic rollback on bad traffic | **yes** (5xx, restarts, health) | no (health check at deploy) | no | no | varies | no | not by default |
| Multiple servers | small groups, canary, labels | yes, by role/host | one host; other schedulers via plugins | yes | their regions | by hand | yes, at any scale |
| Needs a Dockerfile | yes | yes | no (buildpacks too) | no (buildpacks too) | no | yes | yes |
| Persistent volumes for the app | named volumes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Web UI | no | no | no (CLI) | **yes** | yes | no | dashboards |
| Where it runs | your Linux servers | your Linux servers | your Linux server | your Linux servers | their servers | yours | yours or managed |
| Leaving | `export` to Kamal, Compose, k8s, Fly | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |

## What appdeploy does differently

**The server drives the deploy.** In a tool where your laptop or CI sequences SSH commands, an
interrupted session can leave a server half-way and a lock behind. In appdeploy your terminal only
watches: the agent writes every step to a journal before running it, finishes after you disconnect,
and finishes or reverts after its own crash.

**It watches the release after the switch.** Health checks before the switch catch apps that do not
start; they do not catch an app that starts and then fails on real requests. appdeploy keeps the old
release running for a few minutes (default 3) and puts traffic back by itself if the new one
produces too many 5xx answers, crashes, or stops answering. Rolling back is a single proxy change.

**No registry, no cross-compiling.** The image is built where it runs (or on a build server) and
copied directly to the other servers. Nothing to host, no credentials to distribute, no `arm64` Mac
building `amd64` images.

**Small groups without a cluster.** Put roles on servers by label; a deploy builds once, goes to
one server first, and a failure undoes the servers already switched. A server that was down catches
up when it returns. Updating appdeploy itself on all servers is one command, in order, with automatic
revert.

**Open at the edges.** Your app needs a Dockerfile, environment variables and `GET /up`; nothing
appdeploy-specific is inside your image. `appdeploy export` renders the live setup for Kamal,
Compose, Kubernetes or Fly. See [Migration](migration.md).

## Compared one by one

**Kamal.** The closest cousin: both deploy Docker images to your servers with a proxy doing zero
downtime switches. Kamal is mature, has a large user base, supports accessories and hooks, handles any
number of servers, and keeps the conductor on your side. Choose Kamal if you already use it, need
volumes, hooks or many servers. Choose appdeploy if you want the server to own the deploy, want
rollbacks driven by traffic, and do not want a registry. The two are close enough that
[migrating between them](migration.md) is mostly renaming.

**Dokku.** A self-hosted Heroku on one server: `git push`, buildpacks or a Dockerfile, plugins for
databases, Let's Encrypt, persistent storage. It is the most similar to appdeploy's workflow and
far more mature, with a large plugin ecosystem. Choose Dokku if you want buildpacks, storage mounts
or plugins. Choose appdeploy if you want automatic rollback, a journaled deploy that survives
crashes, or more than one server.

**Coolify, Dokploy and similar.** Self-hosted platforms with a web UI, templates for many databases
and services, and multi-server support. Choose them if you want a dashboard, a catalogue of
one-click services, or a team that prefers clicking. appdeploy has no UI and does one thing: ship
and run your web apps safely, from the command line and git.

**Fly.io, Render, Railway and other hosted platforms.** Someone else runs the servers; you pay for
that and accept their limits and prices. Choose them if you do not want to operate servers at all.
appdeploy is for when you do (cost, data location, control) and want that to be pleasant.

**Docker Compose with SSH scripts.** Fine for one app, until you need the switch without downtime,
rollbacks, secrets per release, TLS and multiple apps; those are what appdeploy adds, and `export`
will give you a Compose file back if you leave.

**Kubernetes.** The right answer at a scale or complexity appdeploy deliberately does not aim at:
dozens of services, autoscaling, many teams, stateful workloads. Below that it is a lot to run.

## What appdeploy does not do

Be sure none of these is a deal breaker before you adopt it:

- **Only named volumes, on one server, without backups.** Files that survive deploys can live in
  a named volume (`roles.<name>.volumes`); host directories, volume drivers and backups of volumes
  are not supported, and during a deploy the old and the new container share the volume for the
  watch window. Postgres and Redis (with backups) are the better home for important data.
- **No buildpacks.** You provide a Dockerfile.
- **Linux servers and Docker only.** The install script targets Debian and Ubuntu with systemd.
- **No web UI** and no multi-user accounts beyond SSH key roles.
- **Not for large fleets.** Up to about ten servers; no scheduler, no autoscaling, no load
  balancer (you bring one, or DNS).
- **Backups stay on the server** unless you copy them; there is no built-in off-site backup.
- **Young.** Version 0.1: thoroughly tested by its own end-to-end suite against real Docker and
  Caddy, but not yet proven in production, and the install script has not been run on a real server
  by its authors. Pin your expectations accordingly, and keep the exit door in mind: `appdeploy export`.
